title: MATH GAOKAO - 418
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Validate a model by comparing its prediction with observed data using relative error.
questions.question: A population model predicts \(P(t)=1200(1.05)^t\). At \(t=2\), the observed population is \(1320\). If a relative error below \(1\%\) is considered acceptable, which conclusion is mathematically valid?

options.label: A
options.text: The model is invalid because the predicted value exceeds the observed value by \(3\).

options.label: B
options.text: The prediction at this observed point meets the stated acceptance criterion because the relative error is about \(0.23\%\), which is below \(1\%\).

questions.explanation:
The predicted value is \[
\begin{aligned}
P(2)&=1200(1.05)^2 \\
&=1200(1.1025) \\
&=1323
\end{aligned}
\]. The observed value is \(1320\), so the absolute error is \(1323-1320=3\). The relative error is \(\frac{3}{1320}\approx 0.00227=0.227\%\). Since \(0.227\%<1\%\), the model is acceptable under this criterion.
questions.hint: Compute the predicted value, then divide the absolute error by the observed value.

questions.learningObjective: Validate a kinematic model by checking that all terms have the same physical dimensions.
questions.question: A velocity model is \(v=v_0+at\), where \(v\) and \(v_0\) have units \(\text{m/s}\), \(a\) has units \(\text{m/s}^2\), and \(t\) has units \(\text{s}\). Which statement correctly checks the dimensional consistency of the model?

options.label: A
options.text: Both \(v_0\) and \(at\) have units of meters per second, so the model is dimensionally consistent.

options.label: B
options.text: \(at\) has units of meters per second squared, so the model is dimensionally inconsistent.

questions.explanation:
The initial velocity \(v_0\) has units \(\text{m/s}\), while
\[
[at]=(\text{m/s}^2)(\text{s})=\text{m/s}.
\]
Both terms therefore have the same units as \(v\). The distractor forgets the time factor in \(at\). Dimensional consistency is a necessary check; it alone does not establish empirical accuracy.
questions.hint: Multiply the units within each term, then compare the terms that are being added.

questions.learningObjective: Estimate a parameter from data and verify the resulting exponential model.
questions.question: A bacterial population is modeled by \(N(t)=800e^{kt}\), with \(t\) measured in hours. Measurements give \(N(0)=800\) and \(N(3)=2400\). What value of \(k\) makes the model exactly match these two data points?
questions.explanation:
At \(t=0\), the model already gives \(800\). The second point requires
\[
800e^{3k}=2400\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{3k}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=\frac{\ln3}{3}.
\]
The distractor omits division by the elapsed time \(3\).
questions.hint: Use the later observation to form an exponential equation, then take natural logarithms.

questions.learningObjective: Validate a model by checking residuals for systematic bias.
questions.question: A model predicts values \(10,12,14\) at three points. The corresponding observed values are \(11,12,13\). The residuals are defined as observed minus predicted. Which conclusion about this sample is valid?

options.label: A
options.text: The residuals have mean \(0\), so the average signed error at these three points is zero; this alone does not rule out a systematic pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: The model is invalid because the residuals are not all zero.

questions.explanation:
The residuals, defined as observed minus predicted, are
\[
11-10=1,\qquad 12-12=0,\qquad 13-14=-1.
\]
Their mean is
\[
\frac{1+0-1}{3}=0.
\]
Thus A is correct: the average signed error is zero. However, positive and negative residuals can cancel, and the sequence \(1,0,-1\) may indicate a pattern if the points are ordered by the predictor. A zero residual mean alone does not establish that a model is free of systematic error. Nonzero residuals alone do not make a model invalid, so B is incorrect.
questions.hint: Compute each residual, then average them.

questions.learningObjective: Validate the appropriate range of a model and avoid unreliable extrapolation.
questions.question: A linear model was validated using data for \(0\le x\le 5\). A student uses it to predict the value at \(x=20\). Which statement about validating this use of the model is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The prediction is reliable because a linear model is valid for all real \(x\).

options.label: B
options.text: Reliability at \(x=20\) is not established by validation on \(0\le x\le5\); this is extrapolation and needs additional evidence.

questions.explanation: The point \(x=20\) lies outside the validated interval \([0,5]\). Using the model there is extrapolation. The relationship may or may not continue beyond the observed range, so validation on \([0,5]\) alone cannot establish the reliability of the prediction at \(20\). This supports B. The fact that a linear formula can be evaluated for all real inputs does not make its real-world predictions valid for all such inputs.
questions.hint: Compare the prediction point with the interval where the model was tested.

questions.learningObjective: Validate a constant-speed assumption from tabulated distance-time data.
questions.question: A model assumes an object moves at a constant speed. The data are \(t=0,1,2,3\text{ s}\) and \(d=0,50,100,150\text{ m}\). Which statement correctly validates the constant-speed assumption for this data set?

options.label: A
options.text: The data support constant speed because the distance increases by \(50\text{ m}\) each second.

options.label: B
options.text: The data reject constant speed because the distance is increasing.

questions.explanation: If speed is constant, equal time intervals produce equal distance increments. Here, from \(0\) to \(1\text{ s}\), \(1\) to \(2\text{ s}\), and \(2\) to \(3\text{ s}\), the increments are \(50,50,50\text{ m}\). Thus the average speed is \(50\text{ m}\text{/s}\) in each interval, supporting the constant-speed assumption.
questions.hint: Check whether the distance increments over equal time intervals are equal.

questions.learningObjective: Validate a model by checking whether its predicted behavior matches the expected monotonic relationship.
questions.question: An investment model is \(A(r)=1000(1+r)^5\), where \(r>0\) is the annual interest rate. Which statement correctly validates the expected behavior of the model?

options.label: A
options.text: The model has the expected rate dependence: \(A(r)\) increases as \(r\) increases.

options.label: B
options.text: The model contradicts the expected rate dependence because \(A(r)\) increases as \(r\) increases.

questions.explanation:
For \(r>0\),
\[
A'(r)=5000(1+r)^4>0.
\]
Thus increasing the interest rate increases the modeled future amount, as expected for this fixed principal and term. This checks the direction of dependence on \(r\); it does not, by itself, validate every assumption of the investment model.
questions.hint: Determine whether \((1+r)^5\) increases or decreases when \(r\) increases.

questions.concept: Continuity Check for a Piecewise Model
questions.learningObjective: Validate a piecewise model at the transition point by checking continuity.
questions.question:
A parking-fee model is
\[
F(t)=
\begin{cases}
2t, & 0\le t\le 3,\\
6+3(t-3), & t>3,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(t\) is in hours. Which statement about the model at \(t=3\) is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The model is continuous at \(t=3\) because the function value and both one-sided limits are \(6\).

options.label: B
options.text: The model has a jump of \(3\) at \(t=3\) because the second formula adds \(6\).

questions.explanation:
The first branch gives \(F(3)=2\cdot3=6\) and a left-hand limit of \(6\). The right-hand limit is
\[
\lim_{t\to3^+}\bigl(6+3(t-3)\bigr)=6.
\]
Both one-sided limits equal \(F(3)\), so the model is continuous there. Its slope changes, but its value does not jump.
questions.hint: Compare the function value at the boundary with the limits obtained from the two sides.

questions.learningObjective: Validate an exponential model by comparing its prediction at a test point with observed data.
questions.question: An exponential model \(y=ab^x\) is fitted using \((0,100)\) and \((1,120)\). At \(x=2\), the observed value is \(150\). If a relative error below \(5\%\) is acceptable, which conclusion is valid?

options.label: A
options.text: The model is not acceptable because its prediction \(144\) differs from \(150\).

options.label: B
options.text: The prediction at this observed point meets the stated acceptance criterion because the relative error is \(4\%\), which is below \(5\%\).

questions.explanation:
From \((0,100)\), \(a=100\). From \((1,120)\), \(100b=120\), so \(b=1.2\). The model predicts \[
\begin{aligned}
y(2)&=100(1.2)^2 \\
&=100(1.44) \\
&=144
\end{aligned}
\]. The observed value is \(150\). The absolute error is \(|150-144|=6\). The relative error is \(\frac{6}{150}=0.04=4\%\), which is below \(5\%\). Therefore the model is acceptable by this criterion.
questions.hint: First determine \(a\) and \(b\), then compute relative error as absolute error divided by observed value.

questions.concept: Dimensional and Behavioral Validation of a Formula
questions.learningObjective: Validate a physical model by checking dimensional consistency and expected dependence.
questions.question: The period of a simple pendulum is modeled by \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\), where \(L\) is length in meters and \(g\) is gravitational acceleration in \(\text{m/s}^2\). Which statement correctly checks the dimensional consistency and predicted dependence of this model? Assume small-angle oscillations and negligible damping.

options.label: A
options.text: The expression is dimensionally consistent and predicts that \(T\) increases when \(L\) increases.

options.label: B
options.text: The expression is dimensionally inconsistent because the square root of \(\frac{L}{g}\) has units of seconds squared.

questions.explanation: The units of \(\frac{L}{g}\) are \(\frac{\text{m}}{\text{m/s}^2}=\text{s}^2\), so \(\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\) has units \(\text{s}\). Thus \(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\) has units of seconds, matching \(T\). Also, for fixed \(g\), increasing \(L\) increases \(\frac{L}{g}\), so \(T\) increases. The model is dimensionally consistent and has the expected dependence on \(L\). These checks are necessary consistency checks, not a substitute for comparison with measurements.
questions.hint: Check the units of \(\frac{L}{g}\) and whether \(T\) becomes larger or smaller as \(L\) grows.
